claims.text: Local chemical ordering enhances preferential atomic bonding in high-entropy nanoalloys.
The degree of local chemical ordering is a primary determinant of high-temperature structural and chemical stability in high-entropy nanoalloys.
Local chemical ordering explains high-temperature stability beyond what can be explained by high configurational entropy alone.
The initial nanoalloys form nearly random, multicomponent high-entropy solid solutions.
Changing elemental ratios or applying targeted doping can enhance local chemical ordering.
Local chemical ordering can be varied while maintaining similar overall configurational entropy.
Temperatures of 700–1000°C are representative of practical high-temperature application conditions for these alloys.
Local chemical order mediates phase integrity and elemental-distribution homogeneity.
Enhanced local chemical ordering raises energetic barriers to atomic diffusion and clustering.
Raised diffusion and clustering barriers reduce elemental segregation and inhibit undesirable phase decomposition during high-temperature exposure.
Compared under identical thermal conditions, alloys with enhanced local ordering will retain a single phase or controlled precipitate structure better than alloys with random atomic arrangements.
Compared under identical thermal conditions, alloys with enhanced local ordering will exhibit less chemical segregation than alloys with random atomic arrangements.
Random as-cast high-entropy nanoalloys typically undergo high-temperature phase decomposition and elemental segregation.
The stability effect of local ordering may depend on composition, processing conditions, and temperature.
